title: Why Genesis Ends With a Funeral
paragraphs:
Why Genesis Ends With a Funeral
The Unexpected Ending That Reveals the Entire Gospel
Most people expect the first book of the Bible to end with triumph.
Instead, Genesis ends with a funeral.
After fifty chapters of creation, covenant, miracles, promises, dreams, rescue, and divine encounters, the final image Scripture leaves us with is startlingly simple:
"So Joseph died, being one hundred and ten years old. They embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt." (Genesis 50:26)
At first glance it almost feels unfinished.
But that is exactly the point.
Genesis ends this way because God wants every reader to feel the ache.
The promise is not yet fulfilled.
And that uncomfortable feeling inside you right now?
That is the feeling Genesis wants you to experience.
Because it is the same feeling every human being carries.
But we live east of it.
The opening chapters of Genesis begin with life.
The Hebrew word for life is חַיִּים (chayyim).
"And He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life." (Genesis 2:7)
Humanity begins with breath from God.
The tragedy of Genesis is not merely that Adam and Eve broke a rule.
It is that humanity lost intimacy with the God who created them.
And from that moment everything changed.
The Hebrew construction intensifies the certainty.
Death was no longer a possibility.
From that moment the rhythm of Genesis becomes haunting.
The phrase echoes through generations like a funeral bell ringing across history.
The book that begins with paradise slowly becomes a cemetery.
Because many people know what it feels like to watch dreams die.
Some people are reading this while carrying grief nobody knows about.
You know what it feels like when life doesn't end the way you expected.
His life was scandal before it became salvation.
Yet somehow God transformed every wound into part of a greater story.
Near the end of Genesis Joseph tells his brothers:
"You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good." (Genesis 50:20)
The Hebrew verb translated "meant" is חָשַׁב (chashav).
It carries the idea of weaving, designing, planning, or crafting.
What humans designed for destruction, God redesigned for redemption.
That is one of the greatest themes in all of Scripture.
Even the great deliverer enters a coffin.
Because Joseph was never the final answer.
Genesis intentionally leaves us longing for someone greater.
Someone who could do more than preserve physical life.
Someone who could defeat death itself.
Someone who could bring humanity home.
Centuries later another man would appear.
His name in Hebrew was יֵשׁוּעַ (Yeshua).
In Greek the New Testament records His name as Ἰησοῦς (Iēsous).
In English we know Him as Jesus.
And unlike Joseph, Jesus did not merely save people from famine.
He came to save them from sin.
The Greek word for sin is ἁμαρτία (hamartia).
Failing to live according to God's design.
Every human being has done this.
The scandal of the Gospel is that God knew this.
The Greek word for loved is ἠγάπησεν (ēgapēsen).
Jesus entered the very story Genesis began.
The One who breathed life into Adam allowed His own breath to leave His body upon a Roman cross.
For a moment it looked like Genesis had won.
The coffin had the final word.
The Greek word Christ uses for resurrection life points toward something Genesis could only anticipate.
That is why Genesis ends with a funeral.
Because God was preparing us to appreciate an empty tomb.
The coffin at the end of Genesis is not the conclusion.
It creates a tension only Jesus can resolve.
Without Genesis 50, the resurrection loses some of its weight.
Without the coffin, we cannot fully appreciate the empty grave.
Without death, we cannot fully understand life.
Without scandal, we cannot fully understand grace.
And perhaps that is where your story intersects with Scripture.
Maybe you are carrying a scandal.
A chapter you wish nobody knew.
You think the story is over.
You think the coffin has already been closed.
But Genesis and the Gospel both declare the same truth:
God sees what His grace can make you become.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel Warrior mission.
If this message stirred your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
What part of your story are you trusting Jesus to rewrite?
Because somewhere tonight, someone is staring at what looks like the end of their story.
And they need to know that with Jesus Christ, coffins are never the final chapter.
The grave could not keep Him, and your past does not have to keep you.
